title: Does a prehabilitation programme help people prepare for heart surgery? A feasibility study
official: Non-randomised mixed-methods feasibility studies to evaluate the delivery, adherence, and acceptability of a prehabilitation programme for patients undergoing cardiac surgery
summary:
Background and study aims
Heart surgery can save lives, but recovery can be difficult. People awaiting heart surgery may have reduced physical fitness, poor nutrition or anxiety, which can make recovery more challenging.
Prehabilitation means supporting people to prepare for surgery. It can include physical activity, nutritional advice and help with emotional wellbeing. Although prehabilitation is used before some other types of surgery, it is not routinely available to people awaiting heart surgery, particularly those already in hospital awaiting urgent surgery.
The Fit4HeartOp Feasibility Study aims to find out whether a personalised prehabilitation programme can be delivered successfully and safely in NHS cardiac surgery services and whether patients and healthcare professionals find it acceptable and practical. The study will also help the researchers decide whether and how to conduct a larger randomised trial in the future.

Who can participate?
Adults aged 18 years or over who have been accepted for cardiac surgery may be eligible.
People undergoing cardiac transplantation and people who are unable to provide informed consent cannot participate.
The study includes:
•	People waiting at home for planned heart surgery (Outpatient feasibility Study).
•	People who are already in hospital awaiting urgent heart surgery (Inpatient feasibility Study).

What does the study involve?
Approximately 60 patients will participate: around 36 in the outpatient study and 24 in the inpatient study.
Everyone receives the Fit4HeartOp prehabilitation programme in addition to their usual NHS care. There is no placebo or control group.
At the beginning of the study, participants complete assessments and questionnaires covering their health, physical function, nutrition, emotional wellbeing and quality of life. A physiotherapist reviews the information to ensure that the programme is appropriate and safe for them.
Participants then receive a personalised programme involving:
•	Physical activity and exercise.
•	Nutritional advice and support.
•	Emotional wellbeing support.
•	Personal goals and an interactive workbook.
•	Regular follow-up contacts. 
Outpatients may participate through local community gym facilities, online sessions or home-based activity. Their programme normally lasts approximately 4-12 weeks. Participants who are already in hospital receive a shorter ward-based programme, normally lasting approximately 1-4 weeks.
Participants complete further questionnaires before surgery and approximately three months after surgery. The research team also collects information about the operation, hospital stay and recovery from participant-completed questionnaires and hospital records.
Some participants may also be invited to optional interviews about their experiences. Healthcare professionals and trained professionals delivering the programme may also be interviewed.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants may benefit from personalised support to improve their physical fitness, nutrition and emotional wellbeing before surgery, although we cannot guarantee that individuals will benefit directly. The information gained from this study will help improve future care for people undergoing cardiac surgery. The main risk is a small possibility of problems related to exercise or physical activity. To minimise this risk, all participants undergo a safety assessment before starting the programme, receive an individualised exercise plan, and are monitored throughout. Taking part also involves completing questionnaires and attending study appointments, which may take time, and some questions may cause temporary emotional distress. Participants can stop taking part at any time without affecting their usual care, and all personal information will be stored securely. 

Patient and public involvement
Patients with experience of cardiac surgery have been involved in designing this study. They helped shape the intervention, informed the design of the interactive workbook, contributed to the choice of outcome measures, and supported the development of a flexible delivery model to ensure accessibility for under-served groups.
They also reviewed participant-facing materials to ensure the study is acceptable and understandable for participants.

Where is the study run from?
The study is coordinated by Bristol Trials Centre at the University of Bristol and is expected to involve NHS cardiac surgery centres in Bristol, Plymouth and Leicester, together with associated referring district general hospitals. The outpatient intervention is delivered in collaboration with Nuffield Health through community facilities, online delivery and other appropriate arrangements.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
January 2027 to August 2027

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research Programme Grants for Applied Research programme, reference NIHR207502.

Who is the main contact?
Fit4HeartOp Study Team, cardiac-prehab@bristol.ac.uk
